narrative.eyebrow: aidataapps · lab 03 · mac plane · development evidence
narrative.title: LogWarden Mac Bench
narrative.subtitle: Eight local model servings auditioning for LogWarden's incident-triage agent on an M4 Max — Foundry Local ONNX arms, Karl's Muse Glimmer conversion in both its ONNX and MLX servings, and MLX-served Gemma 4 variants including the 26B-A4B MoE — scored on sixteen frozen SQL Server incident episodes under the lab's structured-JSON transport.
verdict: The Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE holds the bench's best-decisions crown — now as a three-way tie it shares with Muse Glimmer in both of its servings. All three score 100% on incident class, 100% on the action rubric, 87.5% exact-triple with flawless tools and correct unknown-abstention — and all three miss the same two severity judgment calls (ep12, ep14), which settles those as ground-truth ambiguity. The MoE stays the primary arm on speed: 70 tok/s and 13.8 s per episode.

The serving-stack experiment answered emphatically: Muse 30B via mlx-vlm with its official DFlash drafter reproduces the Foundry ONNX bundle's decisions episode-for-episode while decoding 2.2× faster — 36.9 vs 16.4 tok/s, 24 vs 52 s per episode, with block-diffusion speculation contributing +63% over plain MLX decode and changing nothing about the output. The MLX+DFlash serving is the Muse reference arm. Behind the leaders: Gemma 4 E4B as the fast arm (75% triple at 4.5 s, but it dismissed the unknown-abstention episode), qwen3-8b / OLMo 3 7B as catalog alternates, qwen3-4b for smoke, qwen2.5-0.5b as the floor. Gemma 4 12B remains blocked on the unsupported gemma4_unified architecture.

The cross-model pattern stands, now over eight servings: reasoning-channel models (Muse twice, the MoE) follow the action rubric perfectly and abstain correctly on unknowns; direct-answer models over-escalate and, in E4B's case, guess at what they don't recognize. The reasoning tax is real (~870–970 tokens per episode against E4B's ~51), but it buys exactly the failure modes an incident agent can't afford — and it survives quantization and serving-stack changes untouched.

scoreboard.title: All sixteen episodes, one resident model at a time
scoreboard.lede: Accuracy columns score the final decision against frozen ground truth; contract columns score every model turn against the transport rule "exactly one JSON object, nothing else." Tool columns cover the four episodes whose packet names a required diagnostic. Best value per column in green.

quality.title: Where each model's judgment holds and slips
quality.lede: Class = what happened; severity = how bad; action = what to do about it. Reasoning-channel models (Muse in both servings, the 26B-A4B MoE) follow the action rubric perfectly; E4B tracks it closely; the Foundry catalog models over-escalate severity-high incidents where the rubric reserves escalation for corruption, security, and unknowns.

scatter.title: Quality has a price axis
scatter.lede: Exact-triple accuracy against decode speed (log scale). Point area tracks on-disk model size. The 87.5% row holds three points: the Foundry Muse bundle, its MLX+DFlash serving at 2.2× the pace, and the MoE. E4B holds the direct-answer frontier; the 0.5B proves speed alone is worthless.

grid.title: Sixteen episodes, eight servings
grid.lede: ✓ exact triple · ◐ right class, wrong severity or action · ✗ wrong class · ∅ no decision produced. ⚙ marks episodes requiring a tool round-trip before deciding.

dossiers.title: Gemma 4 26B-A4B — the MoE that ties Muse
dossiers.facts: 18.8 GB · 128 experts · ~4B active · 70 tok/s · MLX 4-bit via mlx_lm.server
dossiers.body: Muse's scoreboard at four times Muse's speed: 100% class, 100% action, perfect tools, and a correct unknown-abstention where E4B guessed. mlx_lm.server splits its reasoning channel into a separate response field (recorded as the legal reasoning_field repair), so the visible reply is always clean JSON. The cost is the reasoning itself: ~968 tokens per episode under the same §A-8 max-tokens override Muse uses.
dossiers.snip:
{"kind":"decision","incidentClass":"unknown","severity":"medium",
 "action":"escalate","rationale":"Application-defined error does not
 match any known SQL Server incident classes."}  ← ep15: correct abstention

dossiers.title: Muse 30B (MLX) — same brain, DFlash wings
dossiers.facts: 18 GB + 5 GB drafter · 36.9 tok/s effective · mlx-vlm 0.6.15 · official DFlash speculation
dossiers.body: The platform-native serving of Karl's reference model, now with the official DFlash block-diffusion drafter Meta ships (muse_glimmer_assistant, supported natively since mlx-vlm 0.6.15): the drafter proposes 16-token blocks the target verifies, adding +63% decode over plain MLX and 2.2× over the Foundry ONNX bundle — with decisions identical in all three servings, including the same two severity judgment calls. mlx-vlm 0.6.15 also splits the reasoning channel into a separate response field, so the visible reply is clean JSON (legal reasoning_field repair). Judgment surviving two quantizations, two serving stacks, and speculative verification bit-for-bit is the bench's strongest robustness evidence.
dossiers.snip:
reasoning_content: …[re-derives the contract, ~880 tokens]…
content: {"kind":"decision","incidentClass":"log_full",
 "severity":"high","action":"open_work_item",…}  ← identical across servings

dossiers.title: Gemma 4 E4B — the late-entrant workhorse
dossiers.body: 75% exact-triple, 100% first-pass-clean JSON, perfect tool discipline, fastest usable decode — the small-model bracket isn't close. Its one real flaw is the dangerous kind: it confidently dismissed the unknown-signal episode as no_incident instead of abstaining and escalating. Different runtime and quantization than the Foundry arms; disclosed, and worth re-checking once a Foundry ONNX Gemma exists.
dossiers.snip:
{"kind":"decision","incidentClass":"no_incident","severity":"low",
 "action":"no_action","rationale":"Application-defined error ... not
 related to core SQL Server infrastructure."}  ← ep15: should abstain

dossiers.title: qwen3-8b — the catalog stalwart
dossiers.body: Best exact-triple among the Foundry catalog models (50%) and the best catalog rubric-follower (75% action). Its one tool blemish is instructive: on ep11 it answered log_full correctly without running the required diagnostic — right answer, docked credit, exactly the required-tool rule the spec warns about.
dossiers.snip:
{"kind":"decision","incidentClass":"log_full","severity":"high",
 "action":"open_work_item","rationale":"Transaction log nearing full
 capacity..."}  ← correct, but skipped get_log_space

dossiers.title: OLMo 3 7B — the clean reader
dossiers.body: 93.8% on class and severity, and 100% first-pass contract — every reply was bare, valid JSON with no reasoning channel to strip. Two habits hold it back: it escalates nearly every high-severity incident against the rubric, and it volunteers diagnostics on 31% of no-tool episodes (then recovers cleanly after the no_data miss).
dossiers.snip:
{"kind":"decision","incidentClass":"login_failure","severity":"high",
 "action":"escalate","rationale":"47 failed sa logins in 5 min from
 unknown host indicates brute-force attack."}  ← first-pass, no repairs

dossiers.title: Muse 30B (Foundry ONNX) — thinks out loud
dossiers.facts: 19.6 GB · ~16 tok/s · load 54 s · custom cache
dossiers.body: The conversion works in the stock daemon, and given room to think it answers almost everything exactly right — but the reasoning channel re-derives the whole contract before every reply, so throughput and token budget dominate. See the budget ablation below.

dossiers.title: qwen3-4b — the fast smoke arm
dossiers.body: 87.5% class accuracy at 1.3 s per episode, perfect tool discipline, zero spurious calls. Weakest on rubric-following (31% action). Its /no_think switch lapsing after a tool result — re-entering the reasoning channel and burning the whole budget — was this bench's first transport finding; the prefix now rides every user turn.
dossiers.snip:
<think> Okay, let's see. The user provided an evidence packet
with a monitoring alert... [512 tokens, never closes]  ← before the fix

dossiers.title: qwen2.5-0.5b — the floor, confirmed
dossiers.body: Emits plausible JSON shapes at ferocious speed and understands nothing: tool_request and decision in the same reply, snake_case keys the schema rejects, apology prose to a frozen snapshot store. Kept as the plumbing control and a useful reminder that shape-validity is not agent capability.

ablation.title: A 30B that thinks out loud, on a token budget
ablation.lede: The INT4 ONNX conversion loads and generates in the stock Foundry daemon — 19 GB resident, ~54 s load, ~16 tok/s — served straight from the mac_bundle cache via foundry cache cd. The catch is the reasoning channel: Muse re-derives the whole operating contract in its thinking channel before answering, so the token budget decides whether an answer exists at all. That is exactly the failure the Lab 03 addendum §A-8 anticipates, and its sanctioned fix is what the headline rows use. The platform-native mlx-vlm serving of the same model with the official DFlash drafter decodes 2.2× faster with identical decisions.

cards.body: Thinking channel exhausts the budget on 13 of 16 episodes; the three answers that fit were all exactly right, and all had to be rescued from reasoning text (contract failures). 15.7 tok/s, ~32 s per episode.

With the addendum-sanctioned reasoning budget and a final-channel parser (to=user message extraction, a legal repair), Muse answers everything: 100% class, 100% action, perfect tools. Mean 853 completion tokens and 52 s per episode — the budget buys correctness, not speed.

narrative.caveatTitle: What this bench is, and is not
caveats: Transport mirrors the lab spec. One user turn carries the byte-identical operating contract (classes, severity and action rubrics, tool schemas) plus the evidence packet; models reply in structured JSON with no native tools parameter; frozen tool snapshots answer tool requests, and a wrong tool gets a deterministic no_data miss (SPEC_ADDENDUM §A-1/§A-3 style). Temperature 0, 512 max tokens, up to 4 model turns.

Disclosed per-model knobs. Qwen3 profiles carry a /no_think prefix on every user turn (the Foundry API has no chat-template kwargs; the prefix lapsing after tool results was itself a bench finding). Muse carries the §A-8 max-tokens override to 1400 and a final-channel parser (to=user<|message|>).

Repair ladder. think/channel/fence/leading-text strips count as legal transport repairs; rescuing a JSON object embedded in prose (balanced_extract) counts as a contract failure even when the rescued decision is right.

Mac-plane evidence only. Foundry serves Microsoft-published ONNX builds (Muse: Karl's conversion) on WebGPU/Metal — different artifacts from the digest-pinned vLLM campaign profiles; nothing here is a frozen-campaign row. One run per model, one seed, 16 hand-authored episodes with authored ground truth; treat gaps under ~10 points as noise, not signal.

Substitutions and runtimes. The Foundry catalog has no Gemma at any size, so all Gemma 4 profiles are mlx-community OptiQ 4-bit conversions served by mlx_lm.server; Muse 30B (MLX) is the mlx-community 4-bit conversion served by mlx_vlm.server 0.6.15 with the official DFlash block-diffusion drafter (meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-assistant) for speculative decoding; Muse is multimodal, so its MLX arch lives in mlx-vlm, not mlx-lm — four runtimes on the bench, disclosed per dossier. mlx_lm.server splits the 26B-A4B MoE's reasoning into a separate message.reasoning field (legal repair); mlx-vlm 0.6.15 splits Muse's reasoning into reasoning_content (legal repair); speculation was verified lossless — plain and speculated runs produced identical decisions. Gemma 4 12B is blocked: every conversion declares gemma4_unified, unsupported by mlx-lm 0.31.3. OLMo ships as OLMo 3 7B Instruct, not the frozen registry's OLMo 3.1 family.
Reproduce: npm run mac:eval -- --profile <key> then npm run mac:report on branch aidataapps-logwarden-mac; rows, metrics, and this page land in the run directory.
